Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 60, verse 1–9 (part 1 of 2):

Surat al-Mumtahanah is Madani and has thirteen verses.
In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.
(p-252) ﴿O you who believe, do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies, offering them affection, when they have disbelieved in what has come to you of the truth, expelling the Messenger and you because you believe in Allah, your Lord. If you have gone out to strive in My cause and seeking My pleasure, [do you] secretly show them affection? I know best what you conceal and what you reveal. And whoever of you does that has certainly strayed from the right way.﴾ ﴿If they overcome you, they will be enemies to you and extend their hands and tongues against you with evil, and they wish you would disbelieve.﴾ ﴿Your relatives and your children will not benefit you on the Day of Resurrection. He will separate between you. And Allah is Seeing of what you do.﴾ ﴿There has already been for you an excellent example in Abraham and those with him, when they said to their people, "Indeed, we are free of you and of what you worship other than Allah. We have rejected you, and there has appeared between us and you enmity and hatred forever until you believe in Allah alone," except for the statement of Abraham to his father, "I will surely ask forgiveness for you, but I have no power for you against Allah. Our Lord, upon You we have relied, and to You we have turned in repentance, and to You is the destination."﴾ ﴿Our Lord, do not make us a trial for those who disbelieve, and forgive us, our Lord. Indeed, You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise.﴾ ﴿There has already been for you in them an excellent example for whoever hopes in Allah and the Last Day. And whoever turns away, indeed Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy.﴾ ﴿Perhaps Allah will place affection between you and those with whom you have [now] enmity from them. And Allah is competent, and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿Allah does not forbid you from those who do not fight you because of religion and do not expel you from your homes—from being righteous toward them and acting justly toward them. Indeed, Allah loves those who act justly.﴾ ﴿Allah only forbids you from those who fight you over religion, expel you from your homes, and aid in your expulsion—[forbids] that you make allies of them. And whoever makes allies of them, it is those who are the wrongdoers.﴾

This surah is Madani. It was revealed concerning Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah, who had sent a letter with a woman to the people of Makkah informing them that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was heading toward them to fight them. Allah informed His Messenger (ﷺ) of that, and he dispatched those who took the letter from the woman. The story is well known in the books of hadith and biography (sirah).

The connection (munasabah) of this surah to what precedes it: when the previous surah mentioned the condition of the hypocrites and the disbelievers, this one opened with the prohibition against allying with the disbelievers and showing them affection. In His saying ﴿My enemy﴾ He added (the pronoun) for emphasis, due to the gravity of their crime and to make known that Allah's punishment will descend upon them. The word ʿaduww (enemy) applies to both the singular and the plural. And ﴿allies﴾ (awliyaʾ) is the second object of ﴿take﴾.

﴿You cast to them affection﴾ (tulqūna ilayhim bil-mawaddah): this is an explanation of their alliance, so it has no place in the i'rab (grammatical analysis), or it is a resumptive statement of information. Al-Hawfi and al-Zamakhshari said: it is a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) from the pronoun in (lā tattakhidhū), or an adjective (ṣifah) of awliyaʾ. This was preceded to by al-Farra', who said: ﴿you cast to them affection﴾ is part of the relative clause (ṣilah) of awliyaʾ. End of quote. In their view, an indefinite noun may take a relative clause, while according to the Basrans it is not given a relative clause but is described (by an adjective). A ḥāl or ṣifah is a restriction, and they were forbidden from taking allies absolutely; the restriction indicates that it would be permissible to take allies when they are not in the state of casting affection, or when the allies do not have this attribute. Yet Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O you who believe, do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies﴾, which shows that the prohibition is not confined to that state or that attribute. Awliyaʾ here is an expression for the conveying of affection, and the object of ﴿you cast﴾ is omitted, meaning: you convey to them the news and secrets of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The bāʾ in ﴿with affection﴾ denotes cause, meaning: because of the affection that exists between them. The Kufans said the bāʾ is extra (ziyadah), as it was said in ﴿and do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:195), meaning: your hands. Al-Hawfi said: the Basrans said it is connected to the verbal noun (maṣdar) implied by the verb, and likewise His saying ﴿with deviation through wrongdoing﴾ (al-Hajj 22:25), meaning: the intention of it with deviation. End of quote. According to this, ﴿with affection﴾ is connected to the verbal noun, meaning: their casting with affection. This is not sound, because it involves omitting the verbal noun (which is relative), and omitting the predicate, since their casting is the subject and what is connected to it (the rest). ﴿And they have disbelieved﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumlah ḥāliyyah), and its referent (dhu al-ḥāl) is the pronoun in ﴿you cast﴾, meaning: you show affection to them, and this is their state, namely disbelief in Allah, and it is not fitting for one who disbelieves in Allah to be loved. Al-Zamakhshari allowed that it be a ḥāl from the subject of (lā tattakhidhū).

Al-Jumhur read ﴿bi-mā jāʾakum﴾, while al-Jahdari and al-Mu'alla from ʿĀṣim read ﴿li-mā﴾ with a lām in place of the bāʾ, meaning: for the sake of what has come to you.

﴿They expel the Messenger﴾: this is a resumptive statement, as an explanation of their disbelief, or a ḥāl from the pronoun in (kafarū). ﴿And you﴾ (wa-iyyākum) is conjoined to ﴿the Messenger﴾. The Messenger was placed before ﴿you﴾ for his honour, and because he is the origin for the believers in him. Had the pronoun been placed first it would have been permissible in Arabic, contrary to one who restricted that to poetic necessity; he said: because you are able to bring it attached, so it is not separated except in necessity. This is refuted by this verse and by His saying: ﴿And We have certainly instructed those who were given the Scripture before you and you, to fear Allah﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:131). He placed the relative here before the addressees because of precedence in time, and for other reasons found in the speech of the Arabs. ﴿That you believe﴾ (an tu'minū) is an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlih), meaning: they expel [you] for your belief, or out of their aversion to your belief. ﴿If you have gone out﴾ (in kuntum kharajtum) is a conditional clause whose response is omitted, due to the indication of what precedes it, namely His saying ﴿do not take My enemy﴾. ﴿Jihadan wa-ibtighaʾ﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun in the position of a ḥāl, meaning: as strivers and seekers, or as an object of purpose.

﴿You secretly show﴾ (tusirrūna): a resumptive statement, meaning: you secretly show [affection] while you know that I know the concealed and the revealed, and I inform the Messenger (ﷺ) of that, so there is no benefit in this deed of yours. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: ﴿tusirrūna﴾ is a substitute for ﴿tulqūna﴾. End of quote. This resembles the substitution of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal), because casting may be secret or open, so it divides into these two types. He also allowed that it be the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimate being: you secretly show. The apparent reading is that ʿalam (know best) is an elative (ism tafḍīl), and for that reason it governs with the bāʾ. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah allowed that it be an imperfect verb governed by the bāʾ, saying: because you say ʿalimtu bi-kadha (I knew of such).

﴿And I know best﴾ is a circumstantial clause. The pronoun in ﴿and whoever of you does it﴾ apparently refers to the nearest previously mentioned item, meaning: whoever does the secret showing. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said it refers to the taking of allies. ﴿Sawāʾ﴾ is in the accusative either as an object (if ḍalla is taken as transitive) or as an adverbial of place, on the estimate of intransitivity. Al-sawāʾ means the middle.

When He forbade the believers from taking the disbelievers as allies, and explained what the alliance consists of in casting affection between them, and mentioned what the disbelievers did to them first, namely expelling the Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers, He mentioned at the end what they would do if they were able to: that if they gain power over you, their enmity toward you will become manifest, and they will extend their hands with killing and torture and their tongues with abuse, and they wish you would revert from your religion, which is the dearest of things to you, and which is the cause of their expelling you. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, how did He bring the response of the condition in the present tense like it, then say ﴿and they wish﴾ in the past tense? I say: the past tense, though in the matter of the condition it is treated like the present in grammatical terms, has a point in it, as if it were said: they wish, before all else, your disbelief and your apostasy, meaning that they intend to inflict upon you the harms of both this world and religion together. End of quote. It seems al-Zamakhshari understood from His saying ﴿and they wish﴾ that it is conjoined to the response of the condition, so he made that a question and answer. What appears is that His saying ﴿and they wish﴾ is not upon the response of the condition, because their wish for your disbelief is not consequent upon gaining power over you and dominating you; rather they wish your disbelief in every state, whether they prevail over you or not. It is instead conjoined to the sentence of condition and consequence, and He informed of two matters: one is the manifestation of their enmity and the extension of hands as mentioned, on the supposition of their gaining power over you, and the other is their wish for your disbelief, not on the supposition of their gaining power over you.

Since Hatib had excused himself by claiming he had kin in Makkah, and so wrote to its people what he wrote so that they would respect him for his kin, Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Your relatives and your children will not benefit you﴾, meaning: your relatives for whose sake you take the disbelievers as allies and draw near to them, defending them. ﴿The Day﴾ (yawm) is an object either of ﴿will benefit you﴾ or of ﴿will separate﴾. Al-Jumhur read ﴿yafṣilu﴾ with a yāʾ, lightened, in the passive voice. Al-Aʿraj, ʿIsa and Ibn ʿĀmir read likewise but with a doubled ṣād; the subject is either ﴿between you﴾, which is built on fatḥah because it is attached to a built noun, or the pronoun of the implied verbal noun in ﴿yafṣilu﴾, meaning: He Himself separates, that is, the separation. ʿĀṣim, al-Ḥasan and al-Aʿmash read yafṣilu with a yāʾ, lightened, active; Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾi and Ibn Thābit read active with a yāʾ, damma, doubled; Abu Ḥaywah and Ibn Abi ʿAblah read likewise but with a nūn, doubled; these two also with Zayd ibn ʿAli read with a nūn, fatḥah, lightened, active; and Abu Ḥaywah also read with a nūn, ḍammah. These are eight readings.

When He forbade alliance with the disbelievers, He mentioned the story of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and that part of his conduct was disassociation from the disbelievers, so that they might take him as a model in that and follow his example. Al-Jumhur read ﴿uswatun﴾ with a kasrah on the hamzah; ʿĀṣim read it with a ḍammah; both are dialects. ﴿And those with him﴾: it was said these are those who believed in him. Al-Tabari and others said: they were prophets contemporary with him, or close to his era, because it is not reported that he had believing followers in his confrontation with them and with Nimrod. Do you not see that he said to Sarah when he migrated to al-Sham, fleeing the land of Nimrod: "There is no one on earth who worships Allah except me and you"? Following Ibrahim, peace be upon him, lies in disassociation from polytheism, and it is in every creed, and with our Messenger (ﷺ) absolutely in beliefs and legal rulings. Al-Jumhur read ﴿bura'a'﴾ as the plural of bari', like ẓarīf and ẓurafā'; ʿĪsā read barā' as a plural of bari' also, like ẓarīf and ẓirāf; Abu Ja'far read it with a ḍammah on the bāʾ, like tu'ām and ẓu'ār, and they are a collective noun (ism jam'), whose singular is bari', tawʾam and ẓi'r; it was transmitted from ʿĪsā. Abu Hatim said: they claimed that ʿĪsā al-Hamdani narrated from him barā' on the pattern fiʿāl, like that in His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am free of what you worship﴾ (al-Zukhruf 43:26) in al-Zukhruf, which is a verbal noun on the pattern fiʿāl that is applied to both singular and plural. Al-Zamakhshari said: and bura'a' on replacing the kasrah with a ḍammah, like rukhāl and rubāb. End of quote. The ḍammah in that is not a substitute for a kasrah, but a原 original ḍammah, and it is close to the patterns of collective nouns, not a broken plural, so the ḍammah is not a substitute for the kasrah.

﴿Except the statement of Ibrahim﴾ is an exception from His saying ﴿an excellent example﴾, as said by Qatadah and al-Zamakhshari. Mujahid, Qatadah, ʿAtaʾ al-Khurasani and others said: the meaning is that the example is for you in this respect and not in the other, because it was for his knowledge that it was not in your situation.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "If his saying, ﴿I will surely ask forgiveness for you﴾, is an exception from the statement that is ﴿a good example﴾, then what about his saying, ﴿And I have no power for you against Allah in anything﴾? It is not fit for exception. Do you not see His saying, ﴿So who has any power for you against Allah in anything?﴾ [al-Fath: 11]?" I say: He intended the exception of the whole statement, "to his father." The intention to promise forgiveness for him, and what follows it, is built upon it and subordinate to it, as if he said: "I will ask forgiveness for you, and I have no ability except to ask forgiveness." End of quote. Al-Zamakhshari also said, first, after mentioning that the exception is from his saying "a good example," in some passages: "Because he intended by the good example that which they were obliged to follow, and to take as a sunnah (a path) by which they guide themselves." End of quote.

What appears to be the case is that it is an exception from a noun governed by Ibrahim: the meaning is, "a good example in the statements of Ibrahim and his disputes with his people, except the saying of Ibrahim to his father, ﴿I will surely ask forgiveness for you﴾, for there is no good example in it." On this view, the exception is muttasil (continuous). As for the view that Ibrahim's saying is included under "a good example," because the meaning of "example" (uswah) is imitation and emulation, the saying is not included under it, but it is included under the statements of Ibrahim, peace be upon him.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is also possible that the exception is from the disavowal and severance that was mentioned, "no part remained except this."

It was also said: It is a munqati' (disjunctive) exception in meaning, meaning that Ibrahim's saying to his father, ﴿I will surely ask forgiveness for you﴾, is not a matter in which you should emulate him, so that you would ask forgiveness and ransom your disbelieving fathers by asking forgiveness.

﴿Our Lord, upon You we have relied﴾ and what follows it. The apparent view is that it is part of Ibrahim's statement, connected with what came before the exception, and it is from among what is to be emulated in him. The exception was placed between them out of care for the exception and because of its closeness to the thing excepted. It is also permissible that it is a command from Allah to the believers, meaning: say, "Our Lord, upon You we have relied," (p-255) He taught them thereby to sever the ties that are between them and the disbelievers.

﴿Our Lord, do not make us a trial for those who disbelieve﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: Do not give them power over us, so that they revile us and torture us. Mujahid said: Do not torture us at their hands, or with a punishment from You, so that they think they are right and we are wrong, and thus they are tested by that. Qatada and Abu Mijlaz said something close to this. The saying of Ibn 'Abbas is stronger, because it is a supplication for themselves, while on the saying of others it is a supplication for the disbelievers. The pronoun in ﴿in them﴾ refers to Ibrahim and those with him. The word "good example" was repeated for emphasis, and this was also reinforced with an oath. And ﴿for whoever hopes﴾ is a badal (substitution) from the pronoun of address, a badal ba'd min kull (substitution of part from whole).

It is related that when this verse was revealed, the Muslims resolved to show enmity to their disbelieving relatives, and grief afflicted them because they had not yet believed so that they might show affection to one another. Then ﴿Perhaps Allah will [bring about] affection﴾ was revealed, as a comfort and as a promise of hope. All of them embraced Islam in the year of the Conquest, and they became brothers. As for the one who mentioned that this affection was the marriage of the Prophet (ﷺ) to Umm Habiba bint Abi Sufyan, and that it occurred after the Conquest, he erred, because her marriage took place at the time of the migration to Abyssinia, and these verses were in the sixth year after the Hijra. That cannot be authentically related from Ibn 'Abbas unless he meant it as an example, even if it preceded this verse, because it continued after the Conquest like the rest of the affections that arose. This was said by Ibn 'Atiyya. "Perhaps" (ʿasā) from Allah the Exalted is certain to occur. ﴿And Allah is All-Powerful﴾ over turning hearts and making the difficult easy. (And Allah is Forgiving) toward those among the polytheists who embrace Islam.

﴿Allah does not forbid you﴾ and the verse. Mujahid said: It was revealed concerning a people in Makkah who believed but did not migrate, and they were in a state of evil because they abandoned the obligation of migration. It was said: It concerns believers from the people of Makkah and elsewhere who abandoned migration. Al-Hasan and Abu Salih said: It concerns Khuza'a, Banu al-Harith ibn Ka'b, Kinana, Muzayna and tribes of the Arabs, who were supporters of the Messenger, loving him and loving his victory. It was said: It concerns those among the disbelievers of Quraysh who did not fight, did not expel, and did not show evil. Qurra al-Hamdani and Ata al-Awfi said: It concerns a people of Banu Hashim, among them al-Abbas. Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr said: It concerns the women and children among the disbelievers. Al-Nahhas and al-Tha'labi said: It means the weak believers who were unable to migrate. It was also said: Her mother, Nufayla bint Abd al-Uzza, who was a polytheist, came to Asma bint Abi Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, with gifts, but she did not accept them and did not permit her to enter. Then the verse was revealed, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded her to let her mother enter her home, to accept from her, to support her, and to be good to her. Ibn 'Atiyya said: The woman, as it is related, was her maternal aunt, and she called her "mother." In al-Tahrir: Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, had divorced his wife Nufayla in the Jahiliyya, and she was the mother of Asma bint Abi Bakr. She came during the period of the truce and gave Asma a pair of earrings and other things, but she disliked accepting them from her, so the verse was revealed.

﴿That you be good to them﴾ and ﴿that you befriend them﴾ are two badal (substitutions) for what precedes them, a badal ishtimal (comprehensive substitution).

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

This surah is Madani. It was revealed concerning Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah, who had sent a letter with a woman to the people of Makkah informing them that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was heading toward them to fight them. The connection (munasabah) of this surah to what precedes it: when the previous surah mentioned the condition of the hypocrites and the disbelievers, this one opened with the prohibition against allying with the disbelievers and showing them affection. This was preceded to by al-Farra', who said: ﴿you cast to them affection﴾ is part of the relative clause (ṣilah) of awliyaʾ. End of quote. In their view, an indefinite noun may take a relative clause, while according to the Basrans it is not given a relative clause but is described (by an adjective). A ḥāl or ṣifah is a restriction, and they were forbidden from taking allies absolutely; the restriction indicates that it would be permissible to take allies when they are not in the state of casting affection, or when the allies do not have this attribute. Yet Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O you who believe, do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies﴾, which shows that the prohibition is not confined to that state or that attribute. This resembles the substitution of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal), because casting may be secret or open, so it divides into these two types. He also allowed that it be the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimate being: you secretly show. The apparent reading is that ʿalam (know best) is an elative (ism tafḍīl), and for that reason it governs with the bāʾ. When He forbade the believers from taking the disbelievers as allies, and explained what the alliance consists of in casting affection between them, and mentioned what the disbelievers did to them first, namely expelling the Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers, He mentioned at the end what they would do if they were able to: that if they gain power over you, their enmity toward you will become manifest, and they will extend their hands with killing and torture and their tongues with abuse, and they wish you would revert from your religion, which is the dearest of things to you, and which is the cause of their expelling you. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, how did He bring the response of the condition in the present tense like it, then say ﴿and they wish﴾ in the past tense? I say: the past tense, though in the matter of the condition it is treated like the present in grammatical terms, has a point in it, as if it were said: they wish, before all else, your disbelief and your apostasy, meaning that they intend to inflict upon you the harms of both this world and religion together. It was said: It concerns believers from the people of Makkah and elsewhere who abandoned migration. Ibn 'Atiyya said: The woman, as it is related, was her maternal aunt, and she called her "mother." She came during the period of the truce and gave Asma a pair of earrings and other things, but she disliked accepting them from her, so the verse was revealed.

﴿That you be good to them﴾ and ﴿that you befriend them﴾ are two badal (substitutions) for what precedes them, a badal ishtimal (comprehensive substitution).

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Al-Aʿraj, ʿIsa and Ibn ʿĀmir read likewise but with a doubled ṣād; the subject is either ﴿between you﴾, which is built on fatḥah because it is attached to a built noun, or the pronoun of the implied verbal noun in ﴿yafṣilu﴾, meaning: He Himself separates, that is, the separation. ʿĀṣim, al-Ḥasan and al-Aʿmash read yafṣilu with a yāʾ, lightened, active; Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾi and Ibn Thābit read active with a yāʾ, damma, doubled; Abu Ḥaywah and Ibn Abi ʿAblah read likewise but with a nūn, doubled; these two also with Zayd ibn ʿAli read with a nūn, fatḥah, lightened, active; and Abu Ḥaywah also read with a nūn, ḍammah. Al-Tabari and others said: they were prophets contemporary with him, or close to his era, because it is not reported that he had believing followers in his confrontation with them and with Nimrod. Do you not see that he said to Sarah when he migrated to al-Sham, fleeing the land of Nimrod: "There is no one on earth who worships Allah except me and you"? The intention to promise forgiveness for him, and what follows it, is built upon it and subordinate to it, as if he said: "I will ask forgiveness for you, and I have no ability except to ask forgiveness." End of quote. Al-Zamakhshari also said, first, after mentioning that the exception is from his saying "a good example," in some passages: "Because he intended by the good example that which they were obliged to follow, and to take as a sunnah (a path) by which they guide themselves." End of quote.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 60, verse 1–9 (part 1 of 2):

Surat al-Mumtahanah is Madani and has thirteen verses.
In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

And whoever of you does that has certainly strayed from the right way.﴾ ﴿If they overcome you, they will be enemies to you and extend their hands and tongues against you with evil, and they wish you would disbelieve.﴾ ﴿Your relatives and your children will not benefit you on the Day of Resurrection. He will separate between you. And Allah is Seeing of what you do.﴾ ﴿There has already been for you an excellent example in Abraham and those with him, when they said to their people, "Indeed, we are free of you and of what you worship other than Allah. We have rejected you, and there has appeared between us and you enmity and hatred forever until you believe in Allah alone," except for the statement of Abraham to his father, "I will surely ask forgiveness for you, but I have no power for you against Allah. Our Lord, upon You we have relied, and to You we have turned in repentance, and to You is the destination."﴾ ﴿Our Lord, do not make us a trial for those who disbelieve, and forgive us, our Lord. Indeed, You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise.﴾ ﴿There has already been for you in them an excellent example for whoever hopes in Allah and the Last Day. And whoever turns away, indeed Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy.﴾ ﴿Perhaps Allah will place affection between you and those with whom you have [now] enmity from them. And Allah is competent, and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿Allah does not forbid you from those who do not fight you because of religion and do not expel you from your homes—from being righteous toward them and acting justly toward them. Indeed, Allah loves those who act justly.﴾ ﴿Allah only forbids you from those who fight you over religion, expel you from your homes, and aid in your expulsion—[forbids] that you make allies of them. And whoever makes allies of them, it is those who are the wrongdoers.﴾

This surah is Madani. It was revealed concerning Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah, who had sent a letter with a woman to the people of Makkah informing them that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was heading toward them to fight them. Allah informed His Messenger (ﷺ) of that, and he dispatched those who took the letter from the woman. The story is well known in the books of hadith and biography (sirah).

In His saying ﴿My enemy﴾ He added (the pronoun) for emphasis, due to the gravity of their crime and to make known that Allah's punishment will descend upon them. This was preceded to by al-Farra', who said: ﴿you cast to them affection﴾ is part of the relative clause (ṣilah) of awliyaʾ. End of quote. In their view, an indefinite noun may take a relative clause, while according to the Basrans it is not given a relative clause but is described (by an adjective). A ḥāl or ṣifah is a restriction, and they were forbidden from taking allies absolutely; the restriction indicates that it would be permissible to take allies when they are not in the state of casting affection, or when the allies do not have this attribute. Yet Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O you who believe, do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies﴾, which shows that the prohibition is not confined to that state or that attribute. Awliyaʾ here is an expression for the conveying of affection, and the object of ﴿you cast﴾ is omitted, meaning: you convey to them the news and secrets of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The bāʾ in ﴿with affection﴾ denotes cause, meaning: because of the affection that exists between them. The Kufans said the bāʾ is extra (ziyadah), as it was said in ﴿and do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:195), meaning: your hands. Al-Hawfi said: the Basrans said it is connected to the verbal noun (maṣdar) implied by the verb, and likewise His saying ﴿with deviation through wrongdoing﴾ (al-Hajj 22:25), meaning: the intention of it with deviation. He also allowed that it be the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimate being: you secretly show. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah allowed that it be an imperfect verb governed by the bāʾ, saying: because you say ʿalimtu bi-kadha (I knew of such).

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

And Allah is Seeing of what you do.﴾ ﴿There has already been for you an excellent example in Abraham and those with him, when they said to their people, "Indeed, we are free of you and of what you worship other than Allah. We have rejected you, and there has appeared between us and you enmity and hatred forever until you believe in Allah alone," except for the statement of Abraham to his father, "I will surely ask forgiveness for you, but I have no power for you against Allah. This surah is Madani. It was revealed concerning Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah, who had sent a letter with a woman to the people of Makkah informing them that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was heading toward them to fight them. The connection (munasabah) of this surah to what precedes it: when the previous surah mentioned the condition of the hypocrites and the disbelievers, this one opened with the prohibition against allying with the disbelievers and showing them affection. This was preceded to by al-Farra', who said: ﴿you cast to them affection﴾ is part of the relative clause (ṣilah) of awliyaʾ. End of quote. In their view, an indefinite noun may take a relative clause, while according to the Basrans it is not given a relative clause but is described (by an adjective). A ḥāl or ṣifah is a restriction, and they were forbidden from taking allies absolutely; the restriction indicates that it would be permissible to take allies when they are not in the state of casting affection, or when the allies do not have this attribute. Yet Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O you who believe, do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies﴾, which shows that the prohibition is not confined to that state or that attribute. Awliyaʾ here is an expression for the conveying of affection, and the object of ﴿you cast﴾ is omitted, meaning: you convey to them the news and secrets of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The bāʾ in ﴿with affection﴾ denotes cause, meaning: because of the affection that exists between them. The Kufans said the bāʾ is extra (ziyadah), as it was said in ﴿and do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:195), meaning: your hands. End of quote. According to this, ﴿with affection﴾ is connected to the verbal noun, meaning: their casting with affection. This is not sound, because it involves omitting the verbal noun (which is relative), and omitting the predicate, since their casting is the subject and what is connected to it (the rest). ﴿And they have disbelieved﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumlah ḥāliyyah), and its referent (dhu al-ḥāl) is the pronoun in ﴿you cast﴾, meaning: you show affection to them, and this is their state, namely disbelief in Allah, and it is not fitting for one who disbelieves in Allah to be loved. Al-Zamakhshari allowed that it be a ḥāl from the subject of (lā tattakhidhū).

Al-Jumhur read ﴿bi-mā jāʾakum﴾, while al-Jahdari and al-Mu'alla from ʿĀṣim read ﴿li-mā﴾ with a lām in place of the bāʾ, meaning: for the sake of what has come to you.

The Messenger was placed before ﴿you﴾ for his honour, and because he is the origin for the believers in him. Had the pronoun been placed first it would have been permissible in Arabic, contrary to one who restricted that to poetic necessity; he said: because you are able to bring it attached, so it is not separated except in necessity. This is refuted by this verse and by His saying: ﴿And We have certainly instructed those who were given the Scripture before you and you, to fear Allah﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:131). He placed the relative here before the addressees because of precedence in time, and for other reasons found in the speech of the Arabs. ﴿That you believe﴾ (an tu'minū) is an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlih), meaning: they expel [you] for your belief, or out of their aversion to your belief. ﴿If you have gone out﴾ (in kuntum kharajtum) is a conditional clause whose response is omitted, due to the indication of what precedes it, namely His saying ﴿do not take My enemy﴾. ﴿Jihadan wa-ibtighaʾ﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun in the position of a ḥāl, meaning: as strivers and seekers, or as an object of purpose.

This resembles the substitution of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal), because casting may be secret or open, so it divides into these two types. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, how did He bring the response of the condition in the present tense like it, then say ﴿and they wish﴾ in the past tense? I say: the past tense, though in the matter of the condition it is treated like the present in grammatical terms, has a point in it, as if it were said: they wish, before all else, your disbelief and your apostasy, meaning that they intend to inflict upon you the harms of both this world and religion together. End of quote. It seems al-Zamakhshari understood from His saying ﴿and they wish﴾ that it is conjoined to the response of the condition, so he made that a question and answer. What appears is that His saying ﴿and they wish﴾ is not upon the response of the condition, because their wish for your disbelief is not consequent upon gaining power over you and dominating you; rather they wish your disbelief in every state, whether they prevail over you or not. It is instead conjoined to the sentence of condition and consequence, and He informed of two matters: one is the manifestation of their enmity and the extension of hands as mentioned, on the supposition of their gaining power over you, and the other is their wish for your disbelief, not on the supposition of their gaining power over you.

Abu Hatim said: they claimed that ʿĪsā al-Hamdani narrated from him barā' on the pattern fiʿāl, like that in His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am free of what you worship﴾ (al-Zukhruf 43:26) in al-Zukhruf, which is a verbal noun on the pattern fiʿāl that is applied to both singular and plural. Al-Zamakhshari said: and bura'a' on replacing the kasrah with a ḍammah, like rukhāl and rubāb. End of quote. The ḍammah in that is not a substitute for a kasrah, but a原 original ḍammah, and it is close to the patterns of collective nouns, not a broken plural, so the ḍammah is not a substitute for the kasrah.

Mujahid, Qatadah, ʿAtaʾ al-Khurasani and others said: the meaning is that the example is for you in this respect and not in the other, because it was for his knowledge that it was not in your situation.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "If his saying, ﴿I will surely ask forgiveness for you﴾, is an exception from the statement that is ﴿a good example﴾, then what about his saying, ﴿And I have no power for you against Allah in anything﴾? Al-Jumhur read ﴿bi-mā jāʾakum﴾, while al-Jahdari and al-Mu'alla from ʿĀṣim read ﴿li-mā﴾ with a lām in place of the bāʾ, meaning: for the sake of what has come to you.

﴿They expel the Messenger﴾: this is a resumptive statement, as an explanation of their disbelief, or a ḥāl from the pronoun in (kafarū). ﴿And you﴾ (wa-iyyākum) is conjoined to ﴿the Messenger﴾. The Messenger was placed before ﴿you﴾ for his honour, and because he is the origin for the believers in him. Had the pronoun been placed first it would have been permissible in Arabic, contrary to one who restricted that to poetic necessity; he said: because you are able to bring it attached, so it is not separated except in necessity. This is refuted by this verse and by His saying: ﴿And We have certainly instructed those who were given the Scripture before you and you, to fear Allah﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:131). He placed the relative here before the addressees because of precedence in time, and for other reasons found in the speech of the Arabs. ﴿That you believe﴾ (an tu'minū) is an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlih), meaning: they expel [you] for your belief, or out of their aversion to your belief. ﴿If you have gone out﴾ (in kuntum kharajtum) is a conditional clause whose response is omitted, due to the indication of what precedes it, namely His saying ﴿do not take My enemy﴾. ﴿Jihadan wa-ibtighaʾ﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun in the position of a ḥāl, meaning: as strivers and seekers, or as an object of purpose.

﴿You secretly show﴾ (tusirrūna): a resumptive statement, meaning: you secretly show [affection] while you know that I know the concealed and the revealed, and I inform the Messenger (ﷺ) of that, so there is no benefit in this deed of yours. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: ﴿tusirrūna﴾ is a substitute for ﴿tulqūna﴾. End of quote. This resembles the substitution of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal), because casting may be secret or open, so it divides into these two types. He also allowed that it be the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimate being: you secretly show. The apparent reading is that ʿalam (know best) is an elative (ism tafḍīl), and for that reason it governs with the bāʾ. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah allowed that it be an imperfect verb governed by the bāʾ, saying: because you say ʿalimtu bi-kadha (I knew of such).

﴿And I know best﴾ is a circumstantial clause. The pronoun in ﴿and whoever of you does it﴾ apparently refers to the nearest previously mentioned item, meaning: whoever does the secret showing. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said it refers to the taking of allies. ﴿Sawāʾ﴾ is in the accusative either as an object (if ḍalla is taken as transitive) or as an adverbial of place, on the estimate of intransitivity. Al-sawāʾ means the middle.

When He forbade the believers from taking the disbelievers as allies, and explained what the alliance consists of in casting affection between them, and mentioned what the disbelievers did to them first, namely expelling the Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers, He mentioned at the end what they would do if they were able to: that if they gain power over you, their enmity toward you will become manifest, and they will extend their hands with killing and torture and their tongues with abuse, and they wish you would revert from your religion, which is the dearest of things to you, and which is the cause of their expelling you. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, how did He bring the response of the condition in the present tense like it, then say ﴿and they wish﴾ in the past tense? I say: the past tense, though in the matter of the condition it is treated like the present in grammatical terms, has a point in it, as if it were said: they wish, before all else, your disbelief and your apostasy, meaning that they intend to inflict upon you the harms of both this world and religion together. End of quote. It seems al-Zamakhshari understood from His saying ﴿and they wish﴾ that it is conjoined to the response of the condition, so he made that a question and answer. What appears is that His saying ﴿and they wish﴾ is not upon the response of the condition, because their wish for your disbelief is not consequent upon gaining power over you and dominating you; rather they wish your disbelief in every state, whether they prevail over you or not. It is instead conjoined to the sentence of condition and consequence, and He informed of two matters: one is the manifestation of their enmity and the extension of hands as mentioned, on the supposition of their gaining power over you, and the other is their wish for your disbelief, not on the supposition of their gaining power over you.

Since Hatib had excused himself by claiming he had kin in Makkah, and so wrote to its people what he wrote so that they would respect him for his kin, Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Your relatives and your children will not benefit you﴾, meaning: your relatives for whose sake you take the disbelievers as allies and draw near to them, defending them. ﴿The Day﴾ (yawm) is an object either of ﴿will benefit you﴾ or of ﴿will separate﴾. Al-Jumhur read ﴿yafṣilu﴾ with a yāʾ, lightened, in the passive voice. Al-Aʿraj, ʿIsa and Ibn ʿĀmir read likewise but with a doubled ṣād; the subject is either ﴿between you﴾, which is built on fatḥah because it is attached to a built noun, or the pronoun of the implied verbal noun in ﴿yafṣilu﴾, meaning: He Himself separates, that is, the separation. ʿĀṣim, al-Ḥasan and al-Aʿmash read yafṣilu with a yāʾ, lightened, active; Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾi and Ibn Thābit read active with a yāʾ, damma, doubled; Abu Ḥaywah and Ibn Abi ʿAblah read likewise but with a nūn, doubled; these two also with Zayd ibn ʿAli read with a nūn, fatḥah, lightened, active; and Abu Ḥaywah also read with a nūn, ḍammah. These are eight readings.

When He forbade alliance with the disbelievers, He mentioned the story of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and that part of his conduct was disassociation from the disbelievers, so that they might take him as a model in that and follow his example. Al-Jumhur read ﴿uswatun﴾ with a kasrah on the hamzah; ʿĀṣim read it with a ḍammah; both are dialects. ﴿And those with him﴾: it was said these are those who believed in him. Al-Tabari and others said: they were prophets contemporary with him, or close to his era, because it is not reported that he had believing followers in his confrontation with them and with Nimrod. Do you not see that he said to Sarah when he migrated to al-Sham, fleeing the land of Nimrod: "There is no one on earth who worships Allah except me and you"? Following Ibrahim, peace be upon him, lies in disassociation from polytheism, and it is in every creed, and with our Messenger (ﷺ) absolutely in beliefs and legal rulings. Al-Jumhur read ﴿bura'a'﴾ as the plural of bari', like ẓarīf and ẓurafā'; ʿĪsā read barā' as a plural of bari' also, like ẓarīf and ẓirāf; Abu Ja'far read it with a ḍammah on the bāʾ, like tu'ām and ẓu'ār, and they are a collective noun (ism jam'), whose singular is bari', tawʾam and ẓi'r; it was transmitted from ʿĪsā. Abu Hatim said: they claimed that ʿĪsā al-Hamdani narrated from him barā' on the pattern fiʿāl, like that in His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am free of what you worship﴾ (al-Zukhruf 43:26) in al-Zukhruf, which is a verbal noun on the pattern fiʿāl that is applied to both singular and plural. Al-Zamakhshari said: and bura'a' on replacing the kasrah with a ḍammah, like rukhāl and rubāb. End of quote. The ḍammah in that is not a substitute for a kasrah, but a原 original ḍammah, and it is close to the patterns of collective nouns, not a broken plural, so the ḍammah is not a substitute for the kasrah.

﴿Except the statement of Ibrahim﴾ is an exception from His saying ﴿an excellent example﴾, as said by Qatadah and al-Zamakhshari. Mujahid, Qatadah, ʿAtaʾ al-Khurasani and others said: the meaning is that the example is for you in this respect and not in the other, because it was for his knowledge that it was not in your situation.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "If his saying, ﴿I will surely ask forgiveness for you﴾, is an exception from the statement that is ﴿a good example﴾, then what about his saying, ﴿And I have no power for you against Allah in anything﴾? It is not fit for exception. Do you not see His saying, ﴿So who has any power for you against Allah in anything?﴾ [al-Fath: 11]?" I say: He intended the exception of the whole statement, "to his father." The intention to promise forgiveness for him, and what follows it, is built upon it and subordinate to it, as if he said: "I will ask forgiveness for you, and I have no ability except to ask forgiveness." End of quote. Al-Zamakhshari also said, first, after mentioning that the exception is from his saying "a good example," in some passages: "Because he intended by the good example that which they were obliged to follow, and to take as a sunnah (a path) by which they guide themselves." End of quote.

What appears to be the case is that it is an exception from a noun governed by Ibrahim: the meaning is, "a good example in the statements of Ibrahim and his disputes with his people, except the saying of Ibrahim to his father, ﴿I will surely ask forgiveness for you﴾, for there is no good example in it." On this view, the exception is muttasil (continuous). As for the view that Ibrahim's saying is included under "a good example," because the meaning of "example" (uswah) is imitation and emulation, the saying is not included under it, but it is included under the statements of Ibrahim, peace be upon him.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is also possible that the exception is from the disavowal and severance that was mentioned, "no part remained except this."

It was also said: It is a munqati' (disjunctive) exception in meaning, meaning that Ibrahim's saying to his father, ﴿I will surely ask forgiveness for you﴾, is not a matter in which you should emulate him, so that you would ask forgiveness and ransom your disbelieving fathers by asking forgiveness.

﴿Our Lord, upon You we have relied﴾ and what follows it. The apparent view is that it is part of Ibrahim's statement, connected with what came before the exception, and it is from among what is to be emulated in him. The exception was placed between them out of care for the exception and because of its closeness to the thing excepted. It is also permissible that it is a command from Allah to the believers, meaning: say, "Our Lord, upon You we have relied," (p-255) He taught them thereby to sever the ties that are between them and the disbelievers.

﴿Our Lord, do not make us a trial for those who disbelieve﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: Do not give them power over us, so that they revile us and torture us. Mujahid said: Do not torture us at their hands, or with a punishment from You, so that they think they are right and we are wrong, and thus they are tested by that. Qatada and Abu Mijlaz said something close to this. The saying of Ibn 'Abbas is stronger, because it is a supplication for themselves, while on the saying of others it is a supplication for the disbelievers. The pronoun in ﴿in them﴾ refers to Ibrahim and those with him. The word "good example" was repeated for emphasis, and this was also reinforced with an oath. And ﴿for whoever hopes﴾ is a badal (substitution) from the pronoun of address, a badal ba'd min kull (substitution of part from whole).

It is related that when this verse was revealed, the Muslims resolved to show enmity to their disbelieving relatives, and grief afflicted them because they had not yet believed so that they might show affection to one another. Then ﴿Perhaps Allah will [bring about] affection﴾ was revealed, as a comfort and as a promise of hope. All of them embraced Islam in the year of the Conquest, and they became brothers. As for the one who mentioned that this affection was the marriage of the Prophet (ﷺ) to Umm Habiba bint Abi Sufyan, and that it occurred after the Conquest, he erred, because her marriage took place at the time of the migration to Abyssinia, and these verses were in the sixth year after the Hijra. That cannot be authentically related from Ibn 'Abbas unless he meant it as an example, even if it preceded this verse, because it continued after the Conquest like the rest of the affections that arose. This was said by Ibn 'Atiyya. "Perhaps" (ʿasā) from Allah the Exalted is certain to occur. ﴿And Allah is All-Powerful﴾ over turning hearts and making the difficult easy. (And Allah is Forgiving) toward those among the polytheists who embrace Islam.

﴿Allah does not forbid you﴾ and the verse. Mujahid said: It was revealed concerning a people in Makkah who believed but did not migrate, and they were in a state of evil because they abandoned the obligation of migration. It was said: It concerns believers from the people of Makkah and elsewhere who abandoned migration. Al-Hasan and Abu Salih said: It concerns Khuza'a, Banu al-Harith ibn Ka'b, Kinana, Muzayna and tribes of the Arabs, who were supporters of the Messenger, loving him and loving his victory. It was said: It concerns those among the disbelievers of Quraysh who did not fight, did not expel, and did not show evil. Qurra al-Hamdani and Ata al-Awfi said: It concerns a people of Banu Hashim, among them al-Abbas. Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr said: It concerns the women and children among the disbelievers. Al-Nahhas and al-Tha'labi said: It means the weak believers who were unable to migrate. It was also said: Her mother, Nufayla bint Abd al-Uzza, who was a polytheist, came to Asma bint Abi Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, with gifts, but she did not accept them and did not permit her to enter. Then the verse was revealed, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded her to let her mother enter her home, to accept from her, to support her, and to be good to her. Ibn 'Atiyya said: The woman, as it is related, was her maternal aunt, and she called her "mother." In al-Tahrir: Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, had divorced his wife Nufayla in the Jahiliyya, and she was the mother of Asma bint Abi Bakr. She came during the period of the truce and gave Asma a pair of earrings and other things, but she disliked accepting them from her, so the verse was revealed.

﴿That you be good to them﴾ and ﴿that you befriend them﴾ are two badal (substitutions) for what precedes them, a badal ishtimal (comprehensive substitution).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 60, verse 10–13 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿O you who have believed, when believing women come to you as emigrants, examine them. Allah is most knowing of their faith. And if you know them to be believers, then do not return them to the disbelievers; they are not lawful for them, nor are they lawful for them. And give the disbelievers what they spent. And there is no blame upon you in marrying them when you have given them their bridal payments. And do not hold on to marriage bonds with disbelieving women. And ask for what you have spent, and let them ask for what they have spent. That is the judgment of Allah; He judges between you, and Allah is Knowing and Wise.﴾ ﴿And if you lose any of your wives to the disbelievers and then you have a retaliation, then give those whose wives have gone the like of what they had spent. And fear Allah, in whom you are believers.﴾ ﴿O Prophet, when believing women come to you pledging allegiance to you that they will not associate anything with Allah, nor steal, nor commit adultery, nor kill their children, nor bring a slander they have invented between their hands and their feet, nor disobey you in what is right, then accept their allegiance and ask Allah for forgiveness for them. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, do not make allies of a people with whom Allah has become angry; they have despaired of the Hereafter as the disbelievers have despaired of the companions of the graves.﴾

The treaty of Hudaybiyah had included that whoever came to the people of Makkah from among the Muslims would not be returned to them, and whoever came to the Muslims from among the people of Makkah would be returned to them. "Umm Kulthum, who was the daughter of 'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt, and she was the first woman to emigrate after the emigration of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), came during the truce of Hudaybiyah, and her two brothers 'Umarah and al-Walid went out after her and said: 'O Muhammad, fulfil for us our condition.' She said: 'O Messenger of Allah, the condition of women is weakness, as you know, so you would return me to the disbelievers, who would tempt me away from my religion, and I have no patience.' So Allah annulled the covenant concerning the women and revealed the verse about them, and He judged with a judgment that they all accepted."

It is said: the occasion of its revelation was Subay'ah bint al-Harith al-Aslamiyyah, who came to Hudaybiyah as a Muslim, and her husband Musafir al-Makhzumi came after her. And it is said: Sayfi ibn al-Rahib, who said: "O Muhammad, return my wife to me, for you have stipulated for us that you would return to us whoever comes to you from us, and this is the clay of the document which has not yet dried." So it was revealed as an explanation that the condition applied only to men and not to women.

Abu Nu'aym al-Isfahani mentioned that the occasion of its revelation was Umaymah bint Bishr ibn 'Amr ibn 'Awf, the wife of Hassan ibn al-Dahdahah, and He, may He be exalted, named them "believing women" before they were examined, because of their uttering the word of testimony and because nothing appeared from them that contradicted that, or because they were approaching the firmness of their faith through the examination.

It was read: "muhajirat" in the nominative as a substitute (badal) for "al-mu'minat". Their examination: 'A'ishah said: "by the verse of the pledge of allegiance." It is said: by their testifying that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah. Ibn 'Abbas said: by oath, that she did not go out except out of love for Allah and His Messenger and desire for the religion of Islam. Ibn 'Abbas also, and Mujahid, Qatadah and 'Ikrimah said: she used to be made to swear that she had not emigrated out of hatred for her husband, nor because of a offence she had committed, nor for any reason of worldly aims other than love of Allah and His Messenger and the Last Abode.

﴿Allah is most knowing of their faith﴾: because He, may He be exalted, is the One who is aware of the secrets of hearts and the hidden beliefs. ﴿And if you know them﴾: he applied "knowledge" to the strong assumption arising from the oath and the appearance of signs through leaving the homeland and settling among a people who are not of her people. He made clear the cessation of their return to the disbelievers, who are their husbands, and that is the prohibition between a Muslim woman and a disbeliever.

Ubayy ibn Ka'b? and Talhah read: "la hunna yahillan lahum" (they are not lawful to them, and neither are they lawful to them), and the prohibition was established by this sentence. His saying: ﴿nor are they lawful for them﴾ (p-257) came by way of emphasis and intensifying the sanctity, because if the believing woman is not lawful to the disbeliever, it is known that there is absolutely no lawfulness between them. It is said: His saying ﴿nor are they lawful for them﴾ conveyed the continuation of the ruling between them in the future, as it is in the present so long as they are upon polytheism and the women are upon faith.

﴿And give them what they spent﴾: He commanded that the disbelieving husband be given what he had spent on his wife when she embraced Islam, so that the loss of both the marriage and the wealth is not combined upon him. Ibn 'Abbas said: after examining her, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave her disbelieving husband what he had spent on her, and 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, then married her; and whenever he examined them, he gave their husbands their dowries. Qatadah said: the ruling concerning the return of the dowry applied only to the women of the people of covenant; as for one who has no covenant between himself and the Muslims, the dowry is not returned to him, and the matter is as Qatadah said. Then He negated blame in the Muslims marrying them when they give them their bridal payments. Then Allah, may He be exalted, commanded the believers to separate from their disbelieving wives, the worshippers of idols.

The majority read: ﴿tumsikū﴾, the imperfect of amsaka, like akrama; Abu 'Amr and Mujahid, with a variant from him; Ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan and al-A'raj: the imperfect of massaka with doubling; al-Hasan also, Ibn Abi Layla, and Ibn 'Amir in the narration of 'Abd al-Hamid, and Abu 'Amr in the narration of Mu'adh: tamassakū with the three vowels open, the imperfect of tamassaka with the second element elided, tamassakū; al-Hasan also: tumsikū with a kasra on the sin, the imperfect of masaka, triliteral. Al-Karkhi said: "al-kawafir" includes men and women. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said to him: the grammarians do not see this except in women, the plural of kafirah. He said: Is it not said: a kafirah group (ṭā'ifah kāfirah) and a kafirah company? Abu 'Ali said: so he was struck dumb, and I said: this is a support. End. This al-Karkhi was a Mu'tazili jurist, and Abu 'Ali was a Mu'tazili, so this interpretation pleased him, but it is nothing, for kafirah is not said as a description of men except as following what it describes, or the noun being elided and intended; otherwise, fa'ilah is not pluralised as fawa'il except for the feminine. "Al-'Isam" is the plural of 'ismah, which is the means of remaining in the marriage bond.

﴿And ask for what you have spent﴾: that is, ask the disbelievers for what you have spent on your wives when they fled to them; ﴿and let them ask﴾: that is, the disbelievers ask for what they spent on their wives when they fled to the believers.

When this ruling was established, the Quraysh said, as is related: "We do not accept this ruling, nor do we abide by it, nor shall we pay anyone any dowry." So because of that this other verse was revealed: ﴿And if you lose any﴾, and Allah commanded the believers to pay whoever among the Muslims had a wife who fled, going over to the disbelievers and apostatising from Islam, the amount of her dowry. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: Is there any benefit in the use of "shay'" (anything) in this matter? I say: Yes, the benefit in it is that not a single thing of this kind, however little or insignificant, is left without compensation, as an intensification and strengthening of this ruling. End. Those women who apostatised from the women of the emigrants and joined the disbelievers were: Umm al-Hakam bint Abi Sufyan, the wife of 'Iyad ibn Shaddad al-Fihri; the sister of Umm Salamah, Fatimah bint Abi Umayyah, the wife of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him; 'Abdah bint 'Abd al-'Uzza, the wife of Hisham ibn al-'As; and Umm Kulthum bint Jarwal, also the wife of 'Umar. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned that they were six, and he mentioned Umm al-Hakam, Fatimah bint Abi Umayyah the wife of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, and 'Abdah, and he mentioned that her husband was 'Amr ibn Wadd; and Kulthum and Birwa' bint 'Uqbah, who was under Shammas ibn 'Uthman; and Hind bint Abi Jahl, who was under Hisham ibn al-'As. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave their husbands their dowries from the booty.

The majority read ﴿fa'āqabtum﴾ with an alif; Mujahid, al-Zuhri, al-A'raj, 'Ikrimah, Humayd, Abu Haywah and al-Za'faranI: with the qaf doubled; al-Nakha'i, al-A'raj also, Abu Haywah also, al-Zuhri also, and Ibn Wathhab: with a variant from him, with the qaf light and open; Masruq, al-Nakha'i also, and al-Zuhri also: with it kasra; Mujahid also: fa-a'qabtum on the pattern af'ala, it is said: 'aqaba al-rajul sahibahu fi kadha, meaning each of the two actions followed the other, and it is said: a'qaba, he said:

"And the stingy fighters were lean, and the one who lends to the borrowers did not get a turn"

And 'aqqaba: he obtained a consequence; and al-ta'qib: a raid following a raid; and 'aqaba with the qaf open and kasra, light. Al-Zamakhshari said: fa'āqabtum from al-'uqbah, which is the turn. He likened what was ruled upon the Muslims and the disbelievers, namely the payment by these of the dowries of those women, once, and by those of the dowries of these women, another time, to a matter in which they take turns, as turns are taken in riding and other things; its meaning: then your turn came to pay the dowry.

﴿Then give﴾ to whoever his wife fled to the disbelievers, the like of her dowry from the dowry of the emigrant woman, and they do not give him her disbelieving husband; and likewise from al-Zuhri: he is given from the dowry of whoever joined them. The meaning of a'qabtum: you entered upon the 'aqabah, and 'aqqabtum from 'aqabahu when he followed him, because each of the two alternating follows the other; and likewise 'aqabtum with the lightened form, it is said: 'aqabahu, yu'qibuhu. End. Al-Zajjaj said: fa'āqabtum: you fought them in battle with a retaliation until you took spoils. And the other readings were explained: "la-kānat al-'uqbā lakum": that is, victory would have been yours until you took spoils. The disbelievers, from His saying (ilā al-kuffār), its apparent meaning is generality over all disbelievers; this was said by Qatadah and Mujahid. Qatadah said: then this ruling was abrogated. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is given from the spoils before they are divided into fifths. Al-Zuhri said: from the property of the fay'; and from him: from the dowry of whoever joined us. It is said: the disbelievers are restricted to the people of covenant. Al-Zuhri said: this was applied on the day of the conquest. Al-Thawri said: it is not acted upon today. Muqatil said: it was in the time of the Messenger, then it was abrogated. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this entire verse has had its ruling lifted. Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi the judge said: this was the ruling of Allah, restricted to that time and that incident, by the consensus of the community. Al-Qushayri said: some people said it is still in force to this day.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 60, verses 10–13 (part 2 of 2):

﴿O Prophet, when believing women come to you pledging allegiance to you...﴾: The pledge of the women took place on the second day of the Conquest (of Mecca), at the Mount of Safa, after he had finished the pledge of the men. He was on Safa, and ʿUmar was below him, pledging the women on his command and conveying (his words) to them on his behalf. The hand of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, never touched the hand of a non-mahram woman at all. "Asma' bint Yazid ibn al-Sakan said: I was among the women who were pledging, and I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, extend your hand that we may pledge to you.' The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said to me: 'Indeed, I do not shake hands with women; rather I take their pledge with what Allah took from them.'" Hind bint ʿUtbah was among the women, and he recited the verse to them. When he had established for them that they would not associate anything with Allah, Hind said: "How can we hope that He will accept from us what He did not accept from the men?" She meant that its obligation is clear. When he came to the matter of theft, she said: "By Allah, I take a small amount from the property of Abu Sufyan, and I do not know whether that is lawful for me." Abu Sufyan said: "Whatever you have taken of anything in the past and in what has passed, it is lawful for you." The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, laughed and recognised her, and said to her: "And are you Hind bint ʿUtbah?" She said: "Yes, so pardon what has passed, O Prophet of Allah; may Allah pardon you." He said: ﴿and that they will not commit adultery﴾. She said: "Does a free woman commit adultery?" He said: ﴿and that they will not kill their children﴾. She said: "We raised them when they were small, and you killed them when they were grown." Her son Handhalah ibn Abi Sufyan had been killed on the Day of Badr. ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, laughed until he fell backwards, and the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, smiled. Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 60, verse 10–13 (part 1 of 2):

And if you know them to be believers, then do not return them to the disbelievers; they are not lawful for them, nor are they lawful for them. And give the disbelievers what they spent. And there is no blame upon you in marrying them when you have given them their bridal payments. And do not hold on to marriage bonds with disbelieving women. And ask for what you have spent, and let them ask for what they have spent. That is the judgment of Allah; He judges between you, and Allah is Knowing and Wise.﴾ ﴿And if you lose any of your wives to the disbelievers and then you have a retaliation, then give those whose wives have gone the like of what they had spent. The "reasonable matter" (al-maʿruf) in which they are forbidden to disobey: Ibn ʿAbbas, Anas and Zayd ibn Aslam said: it is wailing, tearing garments, tattooing faces, joining hair, and other matters of the Shariah, whether obligatory or recommended.

It is narrated that some of the poor Muslims used to associate with the Jews in order to obtain some of their fruits, so it was said to them: "Do not take as allies a people upon whom Allah is angry" (and it is said that these are the Jews). Al-Hasan, Ibn Zayd and Mundhir ibn Saʿid explained it thus, because the anger of Allah had become their known attribute. Ibn ʿAbbas said: they are the disbelievers of Quraysh, because every disbeliever has anger from Allah upon him. It has also been said: the Jews and the Christians.

﴿they have despaired of the Hereafter﴾: Ibn ʿAbbas said: of its good and its reward. The apparent meaning is that "min" in ﴿min aṣḥāb al-qubūr﴾ indicates the starting point of the end (ibtidaʾ al-ghayah), i.e., meeting the people of the graves. The second "min" is like the first, in "min al-ākhirah." So the meaning is that they will not meet them in the abode of this world after their death. Ibn ʿArafah said: they are those who said: "Nothing destroys us except time." Ended. The disbelievers in this view are the disbelievers of Mecca, because when a close relative of theirs died they said: "This is the last covenant with him; he will never be resurrected." This is the interpretation of Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatadah and al-Hasan. It has also been said: "min" is explanatory (li-bayan al-jins), i.e., the disbelievers who are the people of the graves, and the thing despaired of is omitted, meaning: just as the disbelievers buried in graves have despaired of the mercy of Allah, because while he was alive and not buried, it was hoped for him that he would not despair of the mercy of Allah, since his faith was expected. This is the interpretation of Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr and Ibn Zayd. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: the explanatory meaning is more evident. Ended. We have already mentioned that the apparent meaning is that "min" indicates the starting point, since the speech does not need an omitted element to be supplied. Ibn Abi al-Zinad read ﴿kamā yaʾisa al-kāfir﴾ in the singular. The majority read it in the plural.

When He opened this surah with the prohibition of taking the disbelievers as allies, He concluded it with the like of that, emphasising the abandonment of their friendship, warning the Muslims against allying with them, and against extending affection to them.
